title: Count the steps, not just the summit
description: Progress you can see keeps you going; measure the actions you control, not only the distant result you do not.

body.heading: Results arrive late and unevenly
paragraphs: Most worthwhile goals have a cruel delay built in. Fitness, fluency, savings, a book — for weeks, the result barely moves no matter how well you work. Judged only by the result, good weeks look identical to wasted ones.
That delay is where many goals quietly die: not from laziness, but from a lack of visible evidence that the effort is doing anything at all.

body.heading: Measure what your hands control
paragraphs: Steps are the actions entirely within your power: sessions done, pages written, minutes practised, small amounts saved. You cannot directly control the summit — the exam grade, the race time, the balance — but you can completely control whether today’s step happens.

Track steps somewhere simple: ticks on a calendar, a tally in a notebook, a jar of pebbles moved from one side to the other. The tracker’s job is to make progress visible on the days the result refuses to.

body.heading: Review steps weekly, results monthly
paragraphs: A rhythm that works: glance at steps weekly (are they happening? does the plan need a repair?), and look at results monthly, with the friend-style review. Steps tell you about the plan; results tell you about the direction. You need both, at different speeds.
And on the discouraging days, the step count is your evidence file. You may not be at the summit. But nobody can argue with forty honest ticks on a calendar.

takeaway: Track the steps you control, and let the summit take care of its own timing.
